skew_join.what: Sort-merge join on a skewed key (50% of rows share one key); the hot partition spills.

diagnosis.verdict: Stage 7 dominates the critical path (64% of wall-clock); binding resource: CPU-bound (JVM compute).

findings.title: Data skew: one task dominates the stage
evidence: Task 13 ran 2,740 ms vs stage median 290 ms (9.4x median, 32% of all task time in the stage).
Input bytes: max task 118.4 MiB vs median 7.7 MiB -> the imbalance is in the DATA, not the node.

MODEL ESTIMATE, UNVALIDATED (replays measured task durations; under-predicted real 4-core times by 38-60% in this repo's validation, so use for direction only) on 16 slots: stage takes 2,751 ms; perfectly balanced it would take 544 ms -> straggler tax 2,207 ms (80% of stage time).
findings.fix: Find the hot key(s). Options in order of preference: (1) broadcast the small side so the hot key never shuffles; (2) enable AQE skew-join (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled) and tune skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes; (3) salt the hot key(s) on the big side and replicate the small side; (4) pre-aggregate before the join.

findings.title: Spill: tasks did not fit their data in execution memory
evidence: 785.0 MiB spilled from memory (260.7 MiB on disk, compressed), in 16 of 16 tasks.
Spilled data is written, then read back and merged: extra disk I/O plus CPU.
findings.fix: Give each task less data (more partitions / fix skew), or more memory per task (fewer cores per executor, larger executor memory / spark.memory.fraction). Prefer the first: it is free.

findings.title: Sort-merge join with a small side that was shuffled
evidence: Join input shuffle sizes: stage 5 wrote 265.9 KiB, stage 6 wrote 232.9 MiB (897x larger).
Both sides were hash-partitioned and sorted across the network although one side would fit in a broadcast (< 128.0 MiB).
findings.fix: Broadcast the small side (F.broadcast(df) or raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold). This removes the shuffle of the big side entirely, and with it any join-key skew.

small_files.what: Scan 1,500 tiny parquet files vs. the same rows compacted to 6 files.

diagnosis.verdict: Stage 4 dominates the critical path (79% of wall-clock); binding resource: CPU-bound (JVM compute).

findings.title: Small-files problem: per-file list/open/footer cost dominates
evidence: Scan read 1,500 files totalling 32.9 MiB -> average file size 22.5 KiB (healthy is 128 MiB to 1 GiB).
6 ms spent listing files / reading metadata on the driver.
findings.fix: Compact into 128 MiB - 1 GiB files (OPTIMIZE on Delta, or a scheduled rewrite job). Fix it at WRITE time (coalesce/repartition before write, or use auto-compaction). Compaction has a one-off cost: it pays back only if the data is read often enough.

over_partitioned.what: groupBy with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=3000 on a ~1 GB-class input.

diagnosis.verdict: Stage 5 dominates the critical path (83% of wall-clock); binding resource: Scheduling / per-task overhead bound.

findings.title: Too many tiny tasks: fixed per-task cost dominates
evidence: 3000 tasks, median duration 6 ms, ~125 B of data per task.
Per-task overhead (deserialise + scheduler delay + result serialisation) is 70% of all task time in this stage.
findings.fix: Reduce partition count to roughly 32 (target 100-200 MiB per task, at least 2-3x the slot count). Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions lower, or enable AQE partition coalescing (spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled).

python_udf.what: Row-at-a-time Python UDF vs. pandas UDF vs. built-in expressions.

stages.name: scan > hash-agg > shuffle-write  [collect@scenarios.py:110]
stages.binding_resource: Waiting on Python workers (UDF serialisation + interpreter)

diagnosis.verdict: Stage 4 dominates the critical path (71% of wall-clock); binding resource: Waiting on Python workers (UDF serialisation + interpreter).

findings.title: Python UDF in the physical plan: rows cross the JVM/Python boundary
evidence: Plan operator: +- BatchEvalPython (5)
Every row is serialised to a Python worker and back; the JVM thread shows up as 'other waiting', not CPU. The optimizer also cannot push filters or prune columns through the UDF.
findings.fix: Replace with built-in Spark SQL functions (F.when, F.regexp_*, F.expr). If logic truly needs Python, use a pandas UDF (Arrow, vectorised) instead of a row-at-a-time UDF.
